subject: chemistry
title: Required practical: chromatography
key_idea: Chromatography separates a mixture of soluble substances. A solvent (the mobile phase) moves through the paper (the stationary phase) and carries each substance a different distance. A pure substance gives one spot. Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.

blocks.text: This section covers the two phases and what makes the substances separate.

items.meaning: The phase that does not move, such as the paper.
The solvent, which moves through the stationary phase.
The paper after the experiment, showing the separated spots.
The furthest point the solvent has reached.

items: Chromatography separates mixtures and helps to identify substances.
Separation depends on how each substance is **distributed between** the two phases.
A substance that spends more time in the mobile phase moves further up the paper.
A substance that is more attracted to the paper spends more time in it, so it moves less far.
Different substances move at different rates, so they end up in different places.
The solvent is the mobile phase; the paper is the stationary phase.
Substances separate because they move at different rates.

blocks.text: This section covers how to separate the colours in an ink. Use the same method for a food colouring.

items: Draw the start line in **pencil**, because ink would dissolve in the solvent and run.
The spot must start above the level of the solvent, or it would dissolve into the beaker.
Put a lid on the beaker so the solvent does not evaporate.
If the ink stays on the start line, use a different solvent so that it dissolves.

diagram.alt: Put the steps of paper chromatography in the right order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of the experiment in order
steps: Draw a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper
Put a small spot of ink on the start line
Pour a little solvent into a beaker, below the level of the spot
Stand the paper in the solvent and put a lid on the beaker
Leave the solvent to travel up the paper
Mark the solvent front and leave the paper to dry
Measure the distances moved by the spots and the solvent

items: Pencil start line, spot above the solvent, lid on.
Mark the solvent front, then leave the paper to dry.

sections.heading: Reading a chromatogram and finding Rf

blocks.text: This section covers what the spots show and how to calculate an Rf value.

items: A **pure substance** gives one spot, whatever solvent is used.
A mixture can give more than one spot.
Known substances are run on the same paper. A spot that moves the same distance as a known substance is likely to be that substance.
The same substance has the same Rf value in the same solvent. Different solvents give different Rf values.

blocks.formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
blocks.label: Rf value
where: distance moved by substance, from the start line to the centre of the spot, in centimetres (cm)
distance moved by solvent, from the start line to the solvent front, in centimetres (cm)

blocks.text: Rf has no units and is always between 0 and 1.

items.text: Measure from the start line to the centre of the spot.
Measure from the start line to the solvent front.

blocks.formula: distance moved by substance = Rf × distance moved by solvent
blocks.label: Distance moved by the substance
where: distance moved by substance in centimetres (cm)
distance moved by solvent in centimetres (cm)

blocks.formula: distance moved by solvent = distance moved by substance ÷ Rf
blocks.label: Distance moved by the solvent
where: distance moved by solvent in centimetres (cm)
distance moved by substance in centimetres (cm)

blocks.text: For example, a spot that moved 3.2 cm with Rf 0.40 means the solvent moved 3.2 ÷ 0.40 = 8.0 cm.

diagram.alt: Calculate an Rf value with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: A dye moves {d} cm from the start line. The solvent front moves {s} cm. Calculate the Rf value of the dye. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
working: Rf = distance moved by dye ÷ distance moved by solvent

items: One spot means pure; more than one spot means a mixture.
Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance.

checks.q: Why is the start line drawn in pencil and not ink?
checks.a: Ink dissolves in the solvent (so the colours of the ink would run and separate).

checks.q: A dye moved 4.5 cm and the solvent front moved 9.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
Explain how chromatography can show that a food colouring contains an unknown dye.
checks.a: Run known dyes and the food colouring on the same paper. Compare the distances moved or the Rf values. A spot that has the same Rf value as a known dye is that dye.

worked_example.question:
Black ink is a mixture of several colours.

Plan an experiment using paper chromatography to:
separate the colours in black ink
identify the colours from their Rf values.
answer_points: Draw a pencil line near the bottom edge of the chromatography paper.
Put a small dot of black ink on the pencil line.
Put a small volume of water or solvent in a beaker.
Place the paper in the solvent, with the dots above the level of the solvent, and support the paper.
Put a lid on the beaker and leave the solvent to run.
Mark the position of the solvent front, then remove the paper and leave it to dry.
Measure the distance of each dot and of the solvent front from the start line, and calculate the Rf values.
Compare the Rf values with known Rf values to identify the colours.
worked_example.tip: A levelled question. Top marks need all the key steps in a logical order, ending with the Rf calculation and the comparison.

worked_example.question:
A scientist uses chromatography in an investigation of compound S.

In the conditions used, compound S has an Rf value of 0.22.

Calculate the distance the spot of compound S moves if the solvent front has moved by 2.4 cm.
answer_points: Rearrange: distance = Rf × distance moved by solvent front.
worked_example.tip: Do not add extra calculation steps: the mark scheme scores 0 for a different method.

blocks.text: The core practical investigates the composition of inks using simple distillation and paper chromatography.

items: The paper chromatography method is the one in this note.
In the experiment, an ink that does not move from the start line needs a different solvent so that it dissolves.

worked_example.question:
A student calculates that a dye has an Rf value of 0.67.

The table shows the Rf value of different dyes.

Colour of dye | Rf value
Blue | 0.15–0.20
Red | 0.35–0.40
Pink | 0.40–0.80
Yellow | 0.75–0.80

Which dye did they use in their experiment?

Explain your answer.
answer_points: The Rf value of 0.67 is in the range 0.40–0.80.
worked_example.tip: Check each row: only one range includes the Rf value.

blocks.text: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) uses a thin layer of solid on a plate as the stationary phase. Gas chromatography uses a gas as the mobile phase.

items: Both types have a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
TLC uses a liquid solvent as the mobile phase. It is used to separate solids.
The mobile phase can be an aqueous or a non-aqueous solvent.
Colourless spots are found using a **locating agent**, a stain or UV light.
Gas chromatography separates gases in a mixture. It shows the amounts of each compound, which TLC does not.
Choose a solvent that dissolves all the substances being separated.

worked_example.question:
A mixture of three amino acids, A, B and C, can be separated and the amino acids identified using paper chromatography.

Complete the equation for Rf, giving the quantity on the top line and on the bottom line of the fraction.

Rf = ______
answer_points: Top line: distance travelled by the substance (M1)
Bottom line: distance travelled by the solvent (M2)

blocks.text: (Supplement) Colourless substances cannot be seen on the paper, so they need a locating agent.

items: Run the chromatogram as usual and let the paper dry.
Spray the paper with a **locating agent**, which reacts with the substances to make them visible.
Measure the distances to the spots, then calculate Rf in the same way.
The names of specific locating agents are not required.

worked_example.question:
A student uses paper chromatography to investigate the dyes in five different inks, V, W, X, Y and Z.

One dye in ink Y moves 4.3 cm when the solvent front moves 6.5 cm.

Calculate the Rf value for this dye. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
answer_points: Rf = distance moved by the dye ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 4.3 ÷ 6.5 (M1)
worked_example.tip: A correct answer to 2 significant figures with no working scores all 3 marks.
